findings.issue_text: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count in BlockedEmail.should_block? causes lost increments under concurrency, and the return value of record.save is ignored so failed stats writes (including last_match_at telemetry) are silently swallowed

EmailValidator performs database writes during validation via BlockedEmail.should_block?, so every User validation with email_changed? inflates match_count even when no signup/block decision is made, and an exception from the auxiliary write (lock timeout, connection issue) aborts the primary operation with a generic 500/error

Blocked-email matching is exact and case-sensitive: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and the unique index don't block case variants like SPAM@evil.com, allowing trivial bypass and duplicate rows; emails should be downcased on write and compared case-insensitively

Client-side rejectedEmails in create_account_controller is populated on any server email error (not just block rejections), masking the server's specific message and permanently failing validation, and it is never reset so the field shows 'invalid' on every reopening until a full page reload

The users_controller signup response sends errors generically with no way for the client to distinguish a block from other email errors, and the joined full_messages in message reveals why the email failed, turning the public signup endpoint into an oracle for probing the site's blocklist

Blocked-email check in BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is case-sensitive and matches raw user-submitted input, allowing admins' blocked emails to be bypassed via case variation or surrounding whitespace (inconsistent with case-insensitive domain blacklist logic in the same validator)
Signup failure response exposes a distinguishable 'user.email.blocked' error, giving unauthenticated users an oracle to enumerate the admin's email blocklist

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (match_count += 1, record.save) inside validation on every user creation, allowing unauthenticated unbounded DB writes; the non-atomic increment loses updates under concurrency and a failed save silently drops the match record while the block decision still returns true

Client infers 'email blocked' from generic errors.email key in create_account_controller.js, conflating blocklist rejections with uniqueness, whitelist/blacklist, and presence validation failures since there is no discriminator distinguishing a block from other email errors

Client permanently adds the address to rejectedEmails (never cleared for the session) and short-circuits with failed: true before the server check, making an address rejected for a transient or fixable reason un-submittable client-side with no recovery path short of a page reload

Message contract divergence: server's translated reason is user.email.blocked ('is not allowed.') but the client renders the generic user.email.invalid, so the user never sees the actual server-provided reason

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs DB writes (match_count += 1, last_match_at, record.save) inside model validation despite being named as a predicate, so any call to user.valid? with a changed email writes to blocked_emails, including callers that only query validity (controllers, background jobs, rake tasks, plugins, tests)
BlockedEmail.should_block? ignores the record.save return value, so a failed save silently loses the stat update

If record.save raises (DB error, unique-index contention on the find-then-save path), the exception propagates out of User#valid? and surfaces as a 500 on the public POST /users signup path instead of a validation failure

The blocked_emails write happens before the User save transaction, so match counts increment even when the surrounding user creation ultimately fails/rolls back — an undocumented behavioral contract for valid?

Public POST /users JSON gains undocumented keys errors (Rails ActiveModel::Errors#to_hash output) and values (sliced attributes hash), making internal Rails representation de-facto public API surface with no versioning or documentation; external consumers will break silently if serialization internals or Rails version change

Case-sensitive block lookup allows trivial bypass of email blocking: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first does an exact case-sensitive match with no downcasing/normalization, so a user blocked as bad@spamclub.com can sign up as Bad@spamclub.com; the client-side rejectedEmails.contains(email) check inherits the same exact-match semantics

Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count in BlockedEmail#should_block? (record.match_count += 1; record.save) causes lost updates under concurrent signups; should use an atomic UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1

record.save return value is ignored so failed stats updates silently vanish with no logging, and if save raises a DB error the exception propagates out of EmailValidator#validate_each turning a routine signup into a 500 — telemetry failure should degrade gracefully and not block account creation

EmailValidator#validate_each performs database writes (SELECT + UPDATE on match_count/last_match_at) inside validation, so any user.valid? call mutates stats; validation should be pure and match accounting belongs in the signup controller/service path

create_account_controller.js pushes result.values.email (the submitted email) into rejectedEmails on failure rather than the field's current value, so if the user edited the email while the request was in flight, a stale address is flagged and the current value may not be marked failed
Tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and only verify one-line wiring, not real behavior; would pass even if should_block? was broken
Moved whitelist/blacklist logic in EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting? (including gsub regex escaping) has zero test coverage
User model validation behavior changed (validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of replaced, email validator delegated) with no User spec changes or end-to-end validation tests
Server→client JSON contract change (errors.to_hash and values.attributes.slice) untested; no controller/request spec verifying payload shape the JS client depends on
Client-side create_account_controller changes (rejectedEmails array, emailValidated branch, observer dependency, pushObject) have no JS tests, including the blocked-email re-validation interaction
BlockedEmail.should_block? exact-match query has no downcasing and no test for mixed-case input, so case variants of blocked emails are not caught
EmailValidator performs no format validation despite its name; no test documents the intended scope of validation (e.g., not-an-email passes)

`action_type` column in create_blocked_emails migration is NOT NULL with no database-level default; the default is only supplied by the before_validation callback in BlockedEmail model, so inserts bypassing ActiveRecord validations will raise a NOT NULL violation

should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count and ignores the return value of save, so concurrent increments can be lost and save failures are silently swallowed; an atomic update_all would fix it

Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and the unique index on blocked_emails.email), allowing trivial blocklist bypass by changing email casing unless the application downcases before validation

EmailValidator performs a DB write as a side effect of validation: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which mutates and saves a row outside the user save transaction, incrementing match_count even when signup fails for unrelated reasons

Blocklist lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? is trivially bypassable via case variation: exact case-sensitive match on where(email: email) with no downcasing anywhere, so 'SPAM@evil.com' variants register cleanly and each case variant is stored as a separate row by the uniqueness index
Trailing whitespace bypass: 'spam@evil.com ' is a different string than the blocked entry and is never format-checked, missing the exact-match blocklist lookup

validates :email, email: true performs no email format validation at all — the validator only checks domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email table, so ' spam@evil.com', 'spam@evil.com.', etc. are all accepted despite the stated goal of comprehensive email validation

BlockedEmail has no attr_accessible, so BlockedEmail.create(email: email) with config.active_record.whitelist_attributes = true raises ActiveModel::MassAssignmentSecurity::UnknownAttributeError, breaking specs and any admin path to populate the blocklist

Client-side rejectedEmails is never cleared and poisons unrelated failures: any server failure with errors.email pushes the email into rejectedEmails, after which emailValid permanently returns invalid for that email for the life of the Ember controller, even after the server-side block is removed

Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count: record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save loses counts under concurrent registration attempts, and the ignored save return value silently drops failed stat updates
The match_count DB write runs inside validation, so any code path calling user.valid? before save double-increments the counter
Removed public methods User#email_validator and User#email_in_restriction_setting? may break external call sites (admin tooling, email-change flows, plugins) with NoMethodError instead of validating

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count in BlockedEmail.should_block? causes lost increments under concurrency, and the return value of record.save is ignored so failed stats writes (including last_match_at telemetry) are silently swallowed

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1` then `record.save`) without any locking/atomic update, so concurrent calls can overwrite each other and lose increments/`last_match_at` updates. Additionally, the `record.save` return value is ignored, so if the save fails (validation/DB error), the method still proceeds to return based on `record.action_type` while silently dropping the intended telemetry updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator performs database writes during validation via BlockedEmail.should_block?, so every User validation with email_changed? inflates match_count even when no signup/block decision is made, and an exception from the auxiliary write (lock timeout, connection issue) aborts the primary operation with a generic 500/error

Blocked-email matching is exact and case-sensitive: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and the unique index don't block case variants like SPAM@evil.com, allowing trivial bypass and duplicate rows; emails should be downcased on write and compared case-insensitively

Client-side rejectedEmails in create_account_controller is populated on any server email error (not just block rejections), masking the server's specific message and permanently failing validation, and it is never reset so the field shows 'invalid' on every reopening until a full page reload

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on any failed signup where `result.errors.email` is present (regardless of which email validation failed), the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Subsequent validations short-circuit on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and return a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, masking the server’s specific email error (e.g. `user.email.not_allowed` vs `user.email.blocked` vs uniqueness). The diff shows no logic to clear `rejectedEmails`, so the same email will continue to be treated as invalid on future attempts within the same controller instance.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The users_controller signup response sends errors generically with no way for the client to distinguish a block from other email errors, and the joined full_messages in message reveals why the email failed, turning the public signup endpoint into an oracle for probing the site's blocklist

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON now includes both `message: ... user.errors.full_messages.join("\n")` and structured `errors: user.errors.to_hash` plus echoed `values` (including `email`). With the new `EmailValidator` adding a distinct `user.email.blocked` error when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true, the public signup endpoint will reveal whether a given email is blocklisted (via `message` and/or `errors.email`), making blocklist membership probeable. The finding’s claim that errors are "generic" is inaccurate (the diff adds `errors`), but the oracle/information-disclosure concern is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-email check in BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is case-sensitive and matches raw user-submitted input, allowing admins' blocked emails to be bypassed via case variation or surrounding whitespace (inconsistent with case-insensitive domain blacklist logic in the same validator)

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact equality lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) on the raw validator input (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` in `EmailValidator#validate_each`) with no normalization (no `strip`, no `downcase`, no case-insensitive query). This makes blocked-email enforcement depend on exact string matching, unlike the domain whitelist/blacklist checks which use a case-insensitive regexp (`Regexp.new(..., true)`), so blocked entries can be bypassed via case/whitespace variations of the same email value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Signup failure response exposes a distinguishable 'user.email.blocked' error, giving unauthenticated users an oracle to enumerate the admin's email blocklist

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new blocked-email check in `EmailValidator` that produces a distinct validation error (`I18n.t('user.email.blocked')`), and `UsersController#create` now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` in the JSON response on signup failure. This allows an unauthenticated client to distinguish “blocked” vs other email failures by probing different emails and inspecting `result.errors.email` / the message, effectively creating an oracle for enumerating the blocked email list (and other restriction reasons).

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (match_count += 1, record.save) inside validation on every user creation, allowing unauthenticated unbounded DB writes; the non-atomic increment loses updates under concurrency and a failed save silently drops the match record while the block decision still returns true

adjudication.rationale: In the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb), a matching record is fetched, then updated via `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save` without checking `save`’s return value and without atomicity. This is a classic read-modify-write race (lost increments under concurrency). Also, this method is invoked from the new `EmailValidator` during user validation (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` in lib/validators/email_validator.rb), so unauthenticated account creation attempts can trigger a DB write on every validation for any email present in `blocked_emails`. If `save` fails, the method still returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, so the block decision can be `true` while the match stats update is silently not persisted.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client infers 'email blocked' from generic errors.email key in create_account_controller.js, conflating blocklist rejections with uniqueness, whitelist/blacklist, and presence validation failures since there is no discriminator distinguishing a block from other email errors

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the client does not infer a specific “email blocked” condition from `errors.email`. It only checks `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` to cache the submitted email in `rejectedEmails`, and then treats any cached rejected email as generically invalid via `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. The server can return different email error messages (e.g., `user.email.blocked`, `user.email.not_allowed`, uniqueness/presence), but the client is not attempting to distinguish “blocked” from other failures—it’s just marking the email as rejected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client permanently adds the address to rejectedEmails (never cleared for the session) and short-circuits with failed: true before the server check, making an address rejected for a transient or fixable reason un-submittable client-side with no recovery path short of a page reload

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the PR introduces `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` and a client-side short-circuit in the email validation: if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` it immediately returns `{ failed: true, reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid') }` before any server-side check. The array is appended to on failed signup responses when `result.errors.email` is present (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), and there is no code in the diff to clear `rejectedEmails` during the session. So an email that triggered a server-side email error once becomes un-submittable client-side until reload, even if the underlying server condition becomes valid later (or the prior failure was transient). This is a real, diff-grounded UX/behavior concern, though not necessarily a strict correctness defect in normal flows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Message contract divergence: server's translated reason is user.email.blocked ('is not allowed.') but the client renders the generic user.email.invalid, so the user never sees the actual server-provided reason

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a mismatch in field-level validation messaging: when a signup fails and `result.errors.email` is present, the controller stores the email in `rejectedEmails`, and subsequent `emailValidation` will always return `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` for that email (see added `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` branch). Meanwhile the server-side validator can add a distinct `user.email.blocked` error (`EmailValidator` adds `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')`). However, the response also includes `message: I18n.t('login.errors', errors: user.errors.full_messages...)`, which would surface the server-provided reason via the flashed `result.message`. So it’s a real UX/contract inconsistency for inline validation, but not strictly “user never sees” the reason in all cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs DB writes (match_count += 1, last_match_at, record.save) inside model validation despite being named as a predicate, so any call to user.valid? with a changed email writes to blocked_emails, including callers that only query validity (controllers, background jobs, rake tasks, plugins, tests)
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core problem: a predicate-style method (should_block_email?/should_block?) has side effects by performing database writes (updating match_count/last_match_at and saving) during what callers expect to be a read-only check, making the name/usage misleading and potentially problematic when invoked from validations or other read-like contexts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? ignores the record.save return value, so a failed save silently loses the stat update

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the method increments `match_count`/sets `last_match_at` and calls `record.save` without checking its boolean return (nor using `save!`). If the save were to fail, the method would still proceed and return based on `action_type`, and the stat update would be silently dropped. This is real and grounded in the diff, but it affects ancillary stats rather than core blocking behavior and the diff doesn’t show a concrete failure case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: If record.save raises (DB error, unique-index contention on the find-then-save path), the exception propagates out of User#valid? and surfaces as a 500 on the public POST /users signup path instead of a validation failure

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds a DB write inside validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` which, on a match, increments fields and does `record.save` without any rescue/handling. Any exception from that `save` (e.g., DB connectivity/locking/constraint issues) would propagate out of the validation path unless caught higher up. However, the finding’s specific mention of “unique-index contention on the find-then-save path” isn’t directly supported here because this code updates an existing row’s counters, not the uniquely-indexed `email` field, and the controller has an existing `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` (not shown how it responds). So the risk is real but the exact failure mode/500 behavior can’t be fully verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The blocked_emails write happens before the User save transaction, so match counts increment even when the surrounding user creation ultimately fails/rolls back — an undocumented behavioral contract for valid?

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no prior email error exists. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates and persists `match_count`/`last_match_at` via `record.save`. This introduces a DB write as a side-effect of validation (`valid?` / `save` validations), so counts can increment even if the `User` ultimately fails other validations and isn’t created. The finding’s specific framing about “before the User save transaction” can’t be fully verified from this diff alone, but the side-effectful validation and potential count inflation is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Public POST /users JSON gains undocumented keys errors (Rails ActiveModel::Errors#to_hash output) and values (sliced attributes hash), making internal Rails representation de-facto public API surface with no versioning or documentation; external consumers will break silently if serialization internals or Rails version change

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes `UsersController#create` failure JSON to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` (see `app/controllers/users_controller.rb`). This does expand the response schema and ties it to Rails’ `ActiveModel::Errors#to_hash` structure, which can be considered an API-surface/compatibility concern even if not a functional defect in-app.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitive block lookup allows trivial bypass of email blocking: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first does an exact case-sensitive match with no downcasing/normalization, so a user blocked as bad@spamclub.com can sign up as Bad@spamclub.com; the client-side rejectedEmails.contains(email) check inherits the same exact-match semantics

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, and neither the model nor the new `EmailValidator` normalizes/downcases `value` before checking. The migration defines `email` as a plain `string` with a unique index, with no case-insensitive collation/citext shown. This makes blocking dependent on exact string match, so a blocked `bad@spamclub.com` would not match `Bad@spamclub.com` under typical DB semantics (e.g., PostgreSQL). The client-side `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` similarly compares the raw input string, so it would not catch case-variants either.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count in BlockedEmail#should_block? (record.match_count += 1; record.save) causes lost updates under concurrent signups; should use an atomic UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on counters: it loads a record, does `record.match_count += 1`, sets `last_match_at`, then `record.save`. Under concurrent calls (e.g., multiple signups hitting the same blocked email), two threads can read the same match_count and overwrite each other’s increment, causing lost updates to match_count (and potentially last_match_at ordering). An atomic UPDATE (`update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or `increment_counter`) would avoid this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: record.save return value is ignored so failed stats updates silently vanish with no logging, and if save raises a DB error the exception propagates out of EmailValidator#validate_each turning a routine signup into a 500 — telemetry failure should degrade gracefully and not block account creation

adjudication.rationale: In the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` method, a matching record triggers a write (`record.save`) during validation without any rescue. While `save` doesn’t raise on validation failure, it can raise on DB-layer exceptions (e.g., `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid`), and `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` with no error handling—so a DB error in the stats update can bubble up and turn signup validation into a 500. Also, the `save` return value is ignored, so failed stat updates can be silently dropped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator#validate_each performs database writes (SELECT + UPDATE on match_count/last_match_at) inside validation, so any user.valid? call mutates stats; validation should be pure and match accounting belongs in the signup controller/service path

adjudication.rationale: Verified: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a lookup and, when a record exists, mutates and persists `match_count`/`last_match_at` via `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This makes `record.valid?` (or any validation run on email changes) have DB-write side effects, which is an architectural/behavioral concern rather than a directly broken behavior shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: create_account_controller.js pushes result.values.email (the submitted email) into rejectedEmails on failure rather than the field's current value, so if the user edited the email while the request was in flight, a stale address is flagged and the current value may not be marked failed

adjudication.rationale: The diff intentionally pushes `result.values.email` (server-echoed submitted email) into `rejectedEmails` on failure, and the validation checks `rejectedEmails.contains(this.get('accountEmail'))`. If the user edits the field while the request is in flight, the response corresponds to the *submitted* email, not necessarily the current UI value—so marking the submitted address as rejected is consistent and avoids incorrectly rejecting the new in-progress value. The finding claims this is a defect, but the diff does not show that the current value *should* be marked failed in that race, nor that storing the submitted value is wrong.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and only verify one-line wiring, not real behavior; would pass even if should_block? was broken

adjudication.rationale: While `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` does stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and only checks that the validator adds/doesn’t add an error based on the stubbed return, the diff also adds `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`, which exercises the real `BlockedEmail.should_block?` behavior (including match_count/last_match_at updates and action_type handling). Therefore the overall tests would *not* pass if `should_block?` were broken, contradicting the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Moved whitelist/blacklist logic in EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting? (including gsub regex escaping) has zero test coverage

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `EmailValidator` with `email_in_restriction_setting?` implementing the whitelist/blacklist domain matching via `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only covers the blocked-email branch by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and does not set `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`blacklist` or exercise `email_in_restriction_setting?`, so that moved restriction logic has no test coverage in this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: User model validation behavior changed (validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of replaced, email validator delegated) with no User spec changes or end-to-end validation tests

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes how User email validation is expressed (replaces `validates_presence_of :email` / `validates_uniqueness_of :email` and `validate :email_validator` with `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` and `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`). While there are new unit specs for `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, there are no specs shown that assert the User model is actually wired to invoke the new validator (and no end-to-end/user-model-level assertions around the new blocked-email behavior). This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap around an altered validation path rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Server→client JSON contract change (errors.to_hash and values.attributes.slice) untested; no controller/request spec verifying payload shape the JS client depends on

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the UsersController#create failure JSON payload to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, and the Ember client now depends on that shape (`result.errors.email` and `result.values.email`) to populate `rejectedEmails`. The added specs cover `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, but there is no controller/request spec asserting this new JSON contract/shape on create failure, so the client-facing API dependency is untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side create_account_controller changes (rejectedEmails array, emailValidated branch, observer dependency, pushObject) have no JS tests, including the blocked-email re-validation interaction

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial client-side logic in `create_account_controller.js` (new `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`, early failure branch `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, observer dependency change to `.property('accountEmail', 'rejectedEmails.@each')`, and `pushObject(result.values.email)` on server-side validation failure). The PR includes only Ruby-side specs (e.g., `email_validator_spec.rb`, `blocked_email_spec.rb`) and no JS/controller tests covering this new re-validation/blocked-email interaction, so the finding about missing JS test coverage is diff-grounded and actionable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? exact-match query has no downcasing and no test for mixed-case input, so case variants of blocked emails are not caught

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization (no `downcase`, no case-insensitive query), and the migration adds a normal unique index on `email` (typically case-sensitive in e.g. Postgres). That means a blocked record for `block@spam.com` will not match `Block@spam.com`, so case variants can bypass blocking. The added specs only stub should_block? and don’t cover mixed-case behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator performs no format validation despite its name; no test documents the intended scope of validation (e.g., not-an-email passes)

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) only enforces domain whitelist/blacklist rules and `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, and does not check that `value` is syntactically an email (e.g., contains `@`, valid format). The added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only documents blocked-email behavior, not whether non-email strings are considered valid/invalid. This is a diff-grounded scope/misleading-name/test-coverage concern rather than a clearly verifiable functional defect, since the previous `User#email_validator` also did not do format validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `action_type` column in create_blocked_emails migration is NOT NULL with no database-level default; the default is only supplied by the before_validation callback in BlockedEmail model, so inserts bypassing ActiveRecord validations will raise a NOT NULL violation

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` with `null: false` but no DB-level `default` (see `20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb`). The only default is set in the model via `before_validation :set_defaults` assigning `self.action_type ||= ...` (in `blocked_email.rb`). That means inserts that bypass validations/callbacks (e.g., raw SQL, `insert_all`, or `create(validate: false)`) could hit a NOT NULL constraint. This is a real, diff-grounded robustness/consistency issue, but not necessarily a runtime defect for standard ActiveRecord creates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count and ignores the return value of save, so concurrent increments can be lost and save failures are silently swallowed; an atomic update_all would fix it

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then mutates `record.match_count += 1` and `record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now` and calls `record.save` without checking the return value. This is a classic non-atomic read/modify/write, so concurrent calls can overwrite each other and lose increments/updates, and a failed `save` would be silently ignored while the method still returns based on `action_type`. An atomic update (e.g., `update_all`/`increment_counter`) and handling `save` failure would address it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) and the unique index on blocked_emails.email), allowing trivial blocklist bypass by changing email casing unless the application downcases before validation
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying issue: BlockedEmail lookup/matching is case-sensitive, so changing email casing (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com) can bypass the blocklist, enabling blocked users to gain access unless emails are normalized (downcased).

adjudication_records.issue_text: EmailValidator performs a DB write as a side effect of validation: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which mutates and saves a row outside the user save transaction, incrementing match_count even when signup fails for unrelated reasons

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces a DB write during validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` mutates `match_count`/`last_match_at` and does `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). That side effect is real and review-worthy (it can cause unexpected writes/perf contention during validations). However, the claim that it occurs “outside the user save transaction” and therefore increments even when signup fails for unrelated reasons is not verifiable from the diff alone (transaction/validation ordering depends on Rails internals not shown here).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocklist lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? is trivially bypassable via case variation: exact case-sensitive match on where(email: email) with no downcasing anywhere, so 'SPAM@evil.com' variants register cleanly and each case variant is stored as a separate row by the uniqueness index

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does a direct `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` lookup with no normalization (no `downcase` on input, no `LOWER(email)` query, no citext), and the `blocked_emails.email` column has a unique index on the raw string. In common Discourse setups (e.g., PostgreSQL text/varchar), comparisons and uniqueness are case-sensitive, so `Spam@evil.com` would not match a row stored as `spam@evil.com` and can bypass the blocklist while also allowing multiple case-variants to exist as separate rows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Trailing whitespace bypass: 'spam@evil.com ' is a different string than the blocked entry and is never format-checked, missing the exact-match blocklist lookup

adjudication.rationale: The new blocklist check is an exact string match with no normalization: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` and the `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` through. Nothing in the diff strips/trims whitespace or normalizes case before lookup, so an entered email like `spam@evil.com ` would not match a stored `spam@evil.com` record and would bypass the new block. (Similarly, the client-side `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` check is also exact-match on the raw string.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: validates :email, email: true performs no email format validation at all — the validator only checks domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email table, so ' spam@evil.com', 'spam@evil.com.', etc. are all accepted despite the stated goal of comprehensive email validation

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `validates :email, email: true` in `User` (app/models/user.rb), backed by the new `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). That validator only enforces domain whitelist/blacklist and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and does not check general email syntax/format (no regex/`Mail::Address` parsing, no trimming). So the finding that this validator provides no format validation is grounded. However, the diff does not show a stated goal of “comprehensive email format validation,” and the prior `email_validator` also only did domain restriction checks, so this is more a misleading/insufficiently-scoped validator than a clearly introduced regression.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BlockedEmail has no attr_accessible, so BlockedEmail.create(email: email) with config.active_record.whitelist_attributes = true raises ActiveModel::MassAssignmentSecurity::UnknownAttributeError, breaking specs and any admin path to populate the blocklist

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail < ActiveRecord::Base` without `attr_accessible`, but nothing in the diff shows `config.active_record.whitelist_attributes = true` (or strict mass-assignment behavior) is enabled. Also, lacking `attr_accessible` would not cause `ActiveModel::MassAssignmentSecurity::UnknownAttributeError` (that error is for non-existent columns); at most it could trigger mass-assignment protection depending on app config, which is not verifiable from this PR diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails is never cleared and poisons unrelated failures: any server failure with errors.email pushes the email into rejectedEmails, after which emailValid permanently returns invalid for that email for the life of the Ember controller, even after the server-side block is removed

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails` is initialized (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`) and `emailValid` unconditionally fails if it `contains(email)`. On any failed signup where `result.errors.email` is present, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(...)`). The diff shows no code path that ever removes/clears entries from `rejectedEmails` during the controller lifetime, so once an email has been rejected by the server once, `emailValid` will keep returning `failed: true` for that same email even if the server-side condition changes (or the error was transient) until the controller is destroyed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count: record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save loses counts under concurrent registration attempts, and the ignored save return value silently drops failed stat updates

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code performs a non-atomic read/modify/write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`). Under concurrent calls for the same email, increments can be lost because each thread reads the same `match_count` then overwrites it. Additionally, the return value of `record.save` is ignored, so failed validations/DB errors would silently drop the stats update while still returning a blocking decision based on `action_type`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The match_count DB write runs inside validation, so any code path calling user.valid? before save double-increments the counter

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no prior email error. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (`app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`). Since validations can run multiple times (e.g., `user.valid?` called more than once before a successful save), this introduces side effects during validation and can increment `match_count` multiple times for a single attempted signup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Removed public methods User#email_validator and User#email_in_restriction_setting? may break external call sites (admin tooling, email-change flows, plugins) with NoMethodError instead of validating

adjudication.rationale: The diff definitively removes the instance methods `User#email_validator` and `User#email_in_restriction_setting?` (previously public) and replaces their behavior with a new ActiveModel `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`) wired via `validates :email, email: true`. If any code outside `User` (e.g., plugins/admin scripts) directly calls those removed methods, it would now raise `NoMethodError`. The diff doesn’t show any such call sites, so the breakage is plausible but not verifiable from the PR alone.
